items.title: Spanish pensioner whose eviction sparked nationwide protests dies, union says
items.tldr: Maricarmen Abascal, an 87‑year‑old Madrid tenant evicted after 70 years in her home, died following a protracted legal battle that ignited nationwide protests over Spain’s housing crisis. Her death has intensified political turmoil, prompting early elections and reigniting debate over emergency housing legislation.
items.background: Spain’s housing market has been under severe pressure for years, driven by soaring rents, limited social housing stock, and speculative investment. The case of Abascal, whose father first rented the property in 1956, became a flashpoint when the new owner, Urbagestión, raised the monthly rent from €500 to €2,650 in 2018. Despite three court‑ordered stays and offers to return at a reduced rate, Abascal could not afford the new terms, leading to a forced eviction on 23 September 2024. The dramatic images of her being removed on a stretcher sparked a wave of public outrage, with thousands camping in Puerta del Sol and demanding affordable‑housing reforms. The political fallout was immediate: the coalition government’s emergency housing bill was rejected, prompting Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez to call a snap election for 29 November 2024.

analysis.heading: Political Repercussions and Electoral Dynamics
analysis.content: Abascal’s death has become a catalyst for political realignment. The governing left‑leaning coalition, already weakened by corruption scandals and cost‑of‑living pressures, saw its housing agenda blocked in Congress, eroding its credibility among progressive voters. Opposition parties, particularly the conservative People’s Party (PP) and the far‑right Vox, have seized the narrative, framing the tragedy as a failure of state intervention. Opinion polls now show the PP edging ahead, though any governing majority would likely require a coalition with Vox, whose hard‑line stance on immigration and regional autonomy could further polarise the legislature. The early election thus pits competing visions of market regulation against calls for stronger tenant protections, with the outcome likely to shape Spain’s approach to housing policy for the next parliamentary term.

analysis.heading: Housing Policy Implications and Legislative Stalled Reform
analysis.content: The tragedy underscores the limits of existing tenant‑protection frameworks. Spain’s 2023 Housing Law caps rent increases for existing contracts, yet it does not prevent owners from substantially raising rents upon purchase, as Urbagestión did. The rejected emergency bill sought to tighten these loopholes, introducing stricter rent caps for new acquisitions and expanding social‑housing subsidies. Its defeat signals a broader ideological clash: right‑wing legislators argue that excessive regulation would deter investment and reduce rental supply, potentially inflating prices further. Meanwhile, advocacy groups and the Madrid Tenants’ Union argue that the cost of inaction—embodied in Abascal’s death—far exceeds any short‑term market distortions. The upcoming parliament will likely revisit these proposals, with the balance of power determining whether a more interventionist stance prevails.

analysis.heading: Societal Impact, Media Narrative, and Grassroots Mobilisation
analysis.content: Abascal’s case has resonated beyond housing policy, becoming a symbol of intergenerational injustice and the erosion of social safety nets. The spontaneous vigil in Puerta del Sol, the “minute of silence” chants, and the march to the Spanish Congress illustrate a deep public yearning for accountability. Social media amplified the story, with hashtags such as #JusticiaParaMaricarmen trending globally, linking local grievances to broader debates on rentierism and urban speculation. The media coverage also highlighted the role of courts and law enforcement in evictions, prompting scrutiny of judicial procedures and police conduct. While the protests have already forced political action, sustaining momentum will require concrete legislative wins and tangible improvements in affordable‑housing availability, otherwise the symbolic power of Abascal’s memory may fade.

key_facts: Maricarmen Abascal, 87, was evicted from her Madrid apartment of over 70 years on 23 September 2024 after rent was raised from €500 to €2,650.
The property was purchased by Urbagestión in 2018; the company later offered a reduced rent of €1,650, still €300 above her monthly pension.
Three previous eviction attempts were blocked by Spanish courts, drawing increasing media attention and public protest.
Her death was announced by the Madrid Tenants’ Union, which described the situation as a turning point in the country’s housing history.
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called a snap election for 29 November 2024 after the emergency housing bill was rejected in Congress.
Protests erupted across Spain, with tens of thousands marching in cities and a continuous occupation of Puerta del Sol lasting more than 12 nights.
implications: Potential shift in Spain’s housing legislation, depending on the election outcome and coalition dynamics.
Increased scrutiny of landlord practices and judicial eviction processes, possibly leading to reforms in tenant rights.
Political advantage for conservative and far‑right parties, which may capitalize on public frustration with the current government’s handling of the crisis.
Heightened public awareness of rent‑inflation pressures, likely to influence future urban planning and social‑housing investment strategies.
items.outlook: The immediate aftermath of Abascal’s death is a charged political environment where housing is the dominant issue. The upcoming election will likely produce a parliament that reflects the public’s demand for action, but the path to consensus remains fraught. If a progressive majority secures power, we can expect swift re‑introduction of stricter rent controls and expanded social‑housing programs. Conversely, a conservative‑led government may prioritize market incentives, potentially delaying reforms. In either scenario, the legacy of Abascal’s struggle will continue to shape Spain’s policy discourse, serving as a cautionary tale of how housing insecurity can ignite broader social and political upheaval.

items.fulltext:
Spanish pensioner whose eviction sparked nationwide protests dies, union says
- Published
An elderly woman whose eviction sparked nationwide protests over Spain's housing crisis and a political row that triggered early elections has died, according to Madrid's tenants union.
Maricarmen Abascal, 87, was forcibly removed on a stretcher from her apartment of more than 70 years on 23 September after she was unable to afford rent increases.
The company that owned the flat later offered to allow her to return at a lower rate - but she was unable to sign an agreement as she had been admitted to hospital.
"We regret to announce that Maricarmen passed away today," the Madrid Tenants' Union said in a statement, adding her situation marked "a turning point in the history of this country".
Union spokesperson Alicia del RÃo said: "Speculation costs lives, and today rentierism has finished killing our colleague Maricarmen" but "her memory lives on with us".
A cause of death was not announced.
Abascal's death was received in Puerta del Sol with a big collective gasp, then followed by a minute of silence.
It is in this square in the centre of Madrid where thousands have been camping since Abascal's eviction last month to demand more affordable housing.
On Wednesday, it became the place to pay tribute to her.
People lit dozens of candles around the square in a small improvised vigil that glowed with a warm light on a dry and warm autumn night.
Other candles formed an altar to Abascal in front of the headquarters of the Community of Madrid government.
Messages on cardboard banners next to the candles read "it's not a death, it's a killing", "the fight will continue" and "Mari Carmen, the grandmother of the whole country", among others.
A few hundred people then took to the streets that connect Puerta del Sol with the Spanish Congress, just 500m away, in an improvised protest.
During the march people chanted: "We will not tolerate a single eviction more" and "the fight will continue, Mari Carmen is still alive". There were other chants against fascism and against the police.
The police had set up barriers to block the march. There was not a big police presence, and there was the tension that protests sometimes have.
Many protesters seemed to feel the police have been complicit in the evictions, as under court orders they have to remove tenants who have been served eviction notices.
After a couple of hours, the chants near Congress gave way to another minute of silence. Then, a big collective shout of "murderers".
Wednesday night's march has finished, but the camping, already on its 12th night, will continue "as long as necessary" one of the protesters told the BBC.
Abascal became a symbol for Spain's housing crisis following her eviction.
Her father first rented the property in 1956 and she continued as the tenant after her parents died, during which time there was a cap on the rent.
However, UrbagestiÃ³n, which bought the property in 2018, increased the rent from â¬500 per month (Â£428; $572) to â¬2,650 (Â£2,280; $3,020).
The company later offered to reduce this to â¬1,650 - still â¬300 more than Abascal's monthly pension.
Three previous attempts to evict her were blocked by the courts and the case has received increasing media attention.
Anger over the situation grew, leading to protests and putting pressure on the coalition government to approve emergency housing legislation - but it was rejected in Congress last week.
That led to further protests, with tens of thousands of people taking to the streets in cities across the country over the weekend.
Referring to the rejected bills, the Madrid Tenants' Union said: "While a historic agreement was reached that would have allowed her to return to her home, this solution has come too late. An absolutely avoidable situation after a torturing process."
It said the events surrounding her eviction represented a turning point in the country's history, but added that the cost to get to this point had been "too high".
"Above all, we will fulfil what she always asked of us: 'fight, keep fighting for what is yours'," it said.
In a video recorded from her hospital bed following her eviction, Maricarmen said: "I haven't managed to defend my home, but I have fought so that others can learn to fight for what's theirs."
"All my love goes to Maricarmen's family and loved ones," Spanish Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez said. "A hug as well to everyone who today feels this loss as their own."
Opposition People's Party leader Alberto NÃºÃ±ez FeijÃ³o also sent his condolences to Maricarmen's loved ones, as he said on X: "No campaign, no parties, no self-interested exploitation. No more stones in the wall.
"In the face of a person's death, only respect is in order," he added.
Earlier on Wednesday, unions had called a general strike to take place on 11 November, demanding housing reforms.
The public outcry over Abascal's situation has led to political turmoil in Spain.
On Monday SÃ¡nchez, who leads a leftist coalition that does not hold a majority in parliament, called an early election for 29 November. It followed his failure to get the emergency housing legislation through Congress.
The political right had argued that the government's attempt to intervene in the housing market would have led to fewer homes being rented and would have raised prices further.
Speaking on Monday, SÃ¡nchez said he needed "a broader progressive majority" that can "overcome the resistance of the elites" to push through reforms.
Other issues not relating to housing, such as numerous corruption scandals linked to his party, and pressures relating to the cost of living and immigration, have also caused him problems.
Most opinion polls suggest the conservatives are likely to emerge as the largest party in the next election. However, they would be expected to need the support of the hard-right Vox party to form a government.

items.title: Israelis mourn 7 October attack victims three years after deadly Hamas raid
items.tldr: On the third anniversary of the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attack, Israel held memorial events honoring the 1,200+ victims and 251 hostages, while political tensions simmer as families demand an independent inquiry and protests highlight security failures.
items.background: The 7 October 2023 assault by Hamas ignited a devastating war in Gaza, killing roughly 1,200 Israelis and abducting 251 hostages. The conflict has claimed over 74,200 Palestinian lives according to the Hamas‑run health ministry, a figure the UN considers credible. A fragile ceasefire brokered almost a year ago has not halted violence, leaving 2.1 million Gazans in dire humanitarian conditions. Three years on, Israel’s political landscape is polarized: families of victims and a growing segment of the public are pressing for a state‑led inquiry into perceived security lapses, while Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government resists an independent commission, citing judicial bias. The anniversary also underscores the broader regional stakes, including the role of emerging technologies—such as AI‑driven surveillance and autonomous weapons—in future conflict prevention and the ongoing debate over tech regulation and open‑source transparency.

analysis.heading: Political Fallout and Domestic Accountability
analysis.content: The anniversary sparked a wave of protests across Israel, with demonstrators demanding an independent state inquiry into the security failures that allowed the Hamas incursion. Prime Minister Netanyahu, facing mounting pressure, has rejected calls for a Supreme Court‑led investigation, arguing that the judiciary would be biased against his administration. Senior defence and security officials have resigned or been dismissed, highlighting a deep institutional rift. The political turbulence is further complicated by the upcoming elections, where the handling of the 7 October tragedy has become a central campaign issue, reshaping coalition dynamics and public trust in the government’s ability to ensure national security.

analysis.heading: Humanitarian and Societal Impact
analysis.content: Memorial ceremonies at sites such as Kibbutz Re’im, the Nova dance festival, and the small cemetery at Kfar Aza brought together bereaved families, survivors, and community leaders. Personal testimonies, including those of Ahuva Yavin Mayze and former hostage Yarden Bibas, underscored the enduring trauma and grief that permeate Israeli society. Community leader Zion Regev noted that many survivors have yet to return to their homes, emphasizing the psychological scars that persist three years later. The collective mourning also extended beyond Israel’s borders, with vigils in Germany, the UK, and other nations, reflecting the global Jewish diaspora’s shared sorrow and solidarity.

analysis.heading: Security Dynamics and Technological Implications
analysis.content: In the aftermath of the raid, Israel has accelerated its reliance on advanced defence systems such as Iron Dome, Arrow, and the upcoming AI‑enhanced aerial surveillance network. The government’s procurement of autonomous drones and AI‑driven threat‑detection platforms has sparked debate over the ethical use of agentic AI in combat zones. Industry analysts point to the growing intersection of defence tech and private‑sector innovation, noting that companies like OpenAI, Gemini, and Anthropic are increasingly involved in research contracts for real‑time battlefield analytics. However, the rapid integration of these technologies raises regulatory concerns, especially as calls for transparency and open‑source verification of algorithmic decision‑making gain traction among civil‑rights groups and international observers.

key_facts: Approximately 1,200 Israelis were killed and 251 taken hostage during the 7 October 2023 Hamas attack.
The Nova dance festival memorial honoured 378 victims, including 21‑year‑old Adi Yavin, whose mother described the event as “dystopic, unimaginable.”
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu lit a memorial candle and vowed to “continue settling the score with all the murderers.”
Over 74,200 people have died in Gaza according to the Hamas‑run health ministry, a figure considered reliable by the UN.
Protests demanding an independent inquiry have led to the resignation or dismissal of several senior defence and security officials.
Israel’s defence budget now includes AI‑driven surveillance and autonomous drone programmes, prompting debate over regulation and open‑source oversight.
implications: The unresolved security failures could erode public confidence in Israel’s defence establishment, influencing future electoral outcomes and policy decisions.
International pressure for an independent inquiry may strain diplomatic relations, especially with allies wary of judicial politicisation.
The expansion of AI and autonomous systems in Israeli defence raises global concerns about the ethical deployment of agentic AI in conflict zones.
Humanitarian conditions in Gaza remain precarious, underscoring the need for sustained diplomatic efforts toward a durable two‑state solution.
items.outlook: The third anniversary highlighted a nation divided between collective remembrance and political contention. While the government continues to pursue military objectives and bolster high‑tech defence capabilities, domestic demands for accountability and international calls for a comprehensive peace framework suggest a complex path ahead. Observers anticipate that the interplay between emerging defence technologies, regulatory debates, and the unresolved trauma of 7 October will shape Israel’s security posture and regional stability for years to come.

Israelis mourn 7 October attack victims three years after deadly Hamas raid
- Published
Memorial events have taken place in Israel on the third anniversary of the devastating Hamas-led attack there that sparked the war in Gaza.
Families paid tribute to their loved ones at some of the sites where about 1,200 people were killed in the assault and 251 were taken hostage.
"The nation unites on this day in the longing for our dear ones," said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faced calls from protesters for an independent state inquiry into security failures that day.
In response to the attack, Israel launched a military offensive in Gaza which has killed more than 74,200 people, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are seen as reliable by the UN.
Violence has continued in Gaza despite a ceasefire agreed almost a year ago and living conditions for the 2.1 million people living there remain dire.
On Wednesday morning, bereaved families and survivors gathered at a memorial for the 378 people who were killed at the Nova dance festival in southern Israel on 7 October 2023.
The festival site was near Kibbutz Re'im and not far from the border with Gaza, from where Hamas-led gunmen launched their dawn attack.
Witnesses have described how festival-goers were shot, sexually abused and tortured by gunmen during the raid.
Forty-four people were kidnapped, of whom 25 were brought back from Gaza alive.
Ahuva Yavin Mayze, whose 21-year-old daughter Adi was shot and killed at Nova, told the BBC what happened at the site was "dystopic, unimaginable".
"Today is a difficult day, not only for me but for a large part of the nation," said Shlomo Sharf, a former Israeli footballer, in comments reported by Channel 12.
He paid tribute to his granddaughter, May Naim, 24, who was also killed at the festival.
Former hostage Yarden Bibas, whose wife and two young sons were kidnapped from their home in Kibbutz Nir Oz and later killed in captivity in Gaza, was quoted by the Times of Israel as saying: "Shiri, Ariel and Kfir. Sorry. Sorry that you are up there and I am here."
Crowds also filed into the small cemetery at Kibbutz Kfar Aza, where 64 residents were killed and 19 were taken hostage on 7 October.
Zion Regev, a community leader, said most surviving residents had yet to return to their homes because of the trauma of what happened.
"This is the first time we are doing all the things here in the kibbutz," he told Reuters news agency. "It's a very emotional day, it's a very difficult day for our community, three years after 7 October."
A man who reportedly helped to fend off Hamas attackers at Kibbutz Magen praised IDF troops who "fought so bravely" during the raid.
Speaking to crowds at the national memorial event at Tel Aviv's Yarkon Park on Wednesday evening, Ido Yakir said Israel would remember everyone "who knew that they had to give their lives in order to save others".
In a statement released by his office on Wednesday afternoon, Netanyahu said he had lit a memorial candle commemorating every victim of 7 October.
"We will complete the mission: we have settled the score and will continue settling the score with all the murderers," he added.
At a ceremony on Monday marking the Jewish calendar's anniversary of the attack, the prime minister said Israel had killed 4,000 out of the 6,000 Palestinians who infiltrated Israel from Gaza that day.
In Tel Aviv's Dizengoff Square, Israeli anti-government protesters dyed the fountain red to mark the anniversary of the attack.
The fountain has been used as a memorial site for those killed, with pictures, flowers and messages laid around the basin wall.
Protesters also briefly blocked one of the main highways in the city to hold a moment of silence on Wednesday morning.
They held banners that read, "the people will remember their sons and daughters", along with others that said "a complete failure" and "guilty" next to an image of Netanyahu.
Many senior Israeli defence and security officials have resigned or been fired since the attack took place. But there has not been an independent commission of inquiry into Israel's worst security failure.
The prime minister has rejected any personal responsibility and has refused to establish a state inquiry led by Israel's Supreme Court, arguing recently that the country's judiciary would be biased against him.
Einav Zangauker became an outspoken critic of the Netanyahu government while her son, Matan, was in captivity in Gaza. He was released last October as part of the ceasefire agreement.
"They're trying to make us forget what happened on 7 October," she told Army Radio. "We won't forget, we will demand the truth."
Memorial events were organised in other countries around the world, including in Germany, where the Jewish students' union held a vigil at Berlin's Brandenburg Gate.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the Hamas-led attack marked a "profound rupture".
"We commemorate the victims, we share their pain," he said, adding that antisemitism must be confronted with "even greater resolve".
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham told Britain's Jewish community: "We stand with you."
"The impact of the attacks has been felt not just in Israel, but in Jewish communities across the world who still bear the burden of the tragic events that day," he said.
Outside Downing Street, a vigil was also held to commemorate British-Israelis killed in the initial attack, later as hostages, or in fighting with Hamas.
Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, said: "The unspeakable savagery and terror of 7 October must never happen again."
She also said that the European Union "remains ready to help turn today's fragile ceasefire into a durable peace, based on a two-state solution."
Speaking to reporters outside the White House on Wednesday, US President Donald Trump said he had spoken to Netanyahu and wished the people of Israel well.
"That was a horrible day, a horrible tragedy," he said.

items.title: Israelis demand accountability over 7 October failures three years after attacks
items.tldr: Three years after the deadliest attacks on Israel since 1948, families and citizens are demanding a state inquiry into the security failures of 7 October 2023. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who refuses personal responsibility, continues his election campaign promising tougher protection, while critics highlight ignored intelligence warnings and a broader policy of containment that may have contributed to the breach.
items.background: On 7 October 2023, Hamas‑led gunmen breached Israel’s border fence, launching a coordinated assault that killed roughly 1,200 Israelis and took another 251 hostages. The attack shattered the country’s sense of security and remains the deadliest incident since the founding of the state in 1948. In the years that followed, survivors, victims’ families, and a growing segment of the public have pressed for an independent state inquiry to examine how the breach was possible. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who was in office at the time, has consistently deflected personal accountability, blaming security chiefs for failing to alert him and asserting that his government’s policy of containment was intended to weaken Hamas. Meanwhile, leaked reports and testimonies suggest that multiple warnings—from female soldiers stationed along the Gaza frontier, from regional neighbours such as the United Arab Emirates, and from Israel’s own intelligence community—were either ignored or not escalated. The absence of a formal investigation has become a focal point in Israeli politics, especially as Netanyahu seeks re‑election on a platform of stronger defence and unwavering resolve.

analysis.heading: Political Accountability and Electoral Implications
analysis.content: The demand for accountability has become a potent political weapon three years after the attacks. Netanyahu’s refusal to order a state inquiry is portrayed by his opponents as an effort to shield himself from culpability and to avoid scrutiny of his government’s strategic choices. The prime minister’s campaign rhetoric—promising to be "stronger and tougher than anyone else" in protecting Israel—contrasts sharply with the perceived failure of his administration to prevent the 7 October breach. Opinion polls indicate a significant portion of the electorate now prioritises transparency and reform over traditional security messaging. This shift could reshape the upcoming election dynamics, potentially fracturing the traditional support base of Netanyahu’s Likud party and opening space for centrist or reform‑oriented parties that champion institutional oversight. Moreover, the political fallout extends beyond Israel’s borders, as allied governments and international observers watch how democratic accountability is exercised in a nation that frames itself as a bastion of security in a volatile region.

analysis.heading: Intelligence Failures and Operational Oversight
analysis.content: A series of revelations points to systemic intelligence lapses that preceded the 7 October assault. Female soldiers posted at forward observation posts along the Gaza border reportedly warned superiors about unusual activity and possible preparations for a large‑scale operation. Their alerts were allegedly down‑ranked or ignored, a pattern echoed in later reports that the UAE’s leadership attempted to call Netanyahu ten days before the attack with specific warnings about Hamas plans. Netanyahu’s office has dismissed these claims as "absolute lies," yet the cumulative effect of ignored warnings raises questions about the decision‑making hierarchy and the culture of information flow within Israel’s security apparatus. Additionally, the policy of "containment"—which allowed Qatar to channel hundreds of millions of dollars in aid to Gaza in the hope of moderating Hamas—has been critiqued as inadvertently bolstering the group’s capabilities. The interplay of political doctrine, budgetary considerations, and operational intelligence suggests a complex web of responsibility that a formal inquiry could disentangle.

analysis.heading: Public Pressure and International Ramifications
analysis.content: Grassroots movements, led by families of the victims, have organized vigils, petitions, and legislative petitions demanding a transparent investigation. Their slogan, "The truth should be clear," reflects a broader societal yearning for closure and assurance that such a catastrophe will not recur. International human‑rights organisations and diplomatic partners have also weighed in, calling for accountability while cautioning against politicising grief. The global spotlight on Israel’s internal governance could affect defence contracts, diplomatic support, and regional alliances, especially as neighbouring states assess the reliability of intelligence sharing and security cooperation. Moreover, the debate over accountability intersects with broader discussions about the ethics of containment policies and the role of external actors—such as the United States and the European Union—in shaping Israel’s security posture.

key_facts: Approximately 1,200 Israelis were killed and 251 taken hostage during the 7 October 2023 Hamas attack, the deadliest since 1948.
Half of Kfar Aza’s 14‑member civil‑defence squad were killed, and four relatives were abducted.
Multiple warnings from female soldiers and alleged UAE intelligence were reportedly ignored or not escalated before the assault.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has refused to order a state inquiry and has blamed security chiefs for not waking him prior to the attacks.
Israel’s policy of containing Hamas—allowing Qatari aid to Gaza—has been criticised as inadvertently strengthening the militant group.
implications: Potential electoral realignment as voters demand transparency and accountability from the incumbent government.
Reassessment of Israel’s intelligence‑sharing protocols and the effectiveness of its containment strategy.
Increased international scrutiny that could affect diplomatic support and defence partnerships.
Renewed public pressure for legislative reforms to ensure oversight of security operations.
items.outlook: The next twelve months are likely to see a convergence of domestic political pressure, judicial processes, and international diplomatic engagement surrounding the call for a state inquiry. If an independent commission is established, its findings could trigger sweeping reforms in Israel’s security doctrine, intelligence dissemination, and civil‑defence coordination. Conversely, continued denial or postponement of accountability may deepen societal divisions, embolden opposition forces, and strain relationships with key allies who value transparent governance. Ultimately, how Israel addresses the legacy of 7 October will shape its internal political landscape and its standing in the broader Middle‑East security architecture.

Israelis demand accountability over 7 October failures three years after attacks
- Published
As the sky began to lighten over Israel's border with Gaza on Wednesday, the people of Kfar Aza moved silently towards the armoury at the centre of the kibbutz.
It was there, shortly after 07:00 on 7 October 2023, that Hamas-led attackers killed half the community's 14-member civil defence squad. They were among 64 killed and 19 kidnapped from the community that day.
The pain of those attacks is still fresh here. But three years on, there are questions about who else should pay the price for Israel's security failure.
"I need my country to take responsibility," said Inbar Goldstein, whose brother and niece were killed, and four other relatives kidnapped from Kfar Aza.
The 7 October attack was the deadliest Israel had suffered since its creation in 1948. About 1,200 people were killed across southern Israel by gunmen who broke through the border fence and attacked communities there. Another 251 people were taken back to Gaza as hostages.
Three years on from Israel's biggest security failure, there is still no independent state inquiry into how it was allowed to happen.
And the man in charge at the time of that failure - Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu - is running for election again, with the same campaign promise: to be stronger and tougher than anyone else in protecting Israel from its enemies.
"Nobody investigated the roots [of the attack]. It didn't start or end on October 7th - it's a long process of abandonment," Goldstein said.
Aside from Hamas's responsibility for the attack itself, there are growing questions in Israel around what caused the country's intelligence failure, what information was passed to military and political leaders in the run-up to the attacks, and what Netanyahu himself knew.
For months beforehand, young female soldiers posted at bases along the Gaza border to watch for suspicious activity had warned their superiors about possible preparations for an attack.
Among them was Roni Eshel. She was killed with 14 other members of her unit when gunmen overran their base at Nahal Oz, just next to Kfar Aza.
"There are so many questions," her uncle Elad Levy told me. "Were the Egyptians warning the prime minister? The Emiratis? Were there no other warnings Netanyahu ignored? We need to find out what happened â not just on the day, but the year before, and five years before that."
"The truth should be clear," he continued. "If we don't inquire into this, it will happen again and again."
- They were Israel's 'eyes on the border' - their warnings went unheard 
  - Published15 January 2024
Over the past three years, there have been mounting reports of warnings being given to Netanyahu - by his own security chief, as well as by regional neighbours â which he denies.
Last month, Israel's Haaretz newspaper published extracts from a new book, alleging that the leader of the United Arab Emirates had called Netanyahu 10 days before the attack to warn of Hamas plans for a major operation.
Netanyahu's office has dismissed the report as "an absolute lie" and has said he will sue the newspaper.
Amir Ohana, a member of Netanyahu's Likud party, said in a social media video last month that it was "preposterous and absurd" to suggest that Netanyahu could have known about the attack when the former Hamas leader in Gaza, Yahya Sinwar, had only told a handful of people.
Israel's prime minister, he said, had since reshaped the Middle East and did not give up, "even when voices inside and outside Israel called on him to stop".
Netanyahu has blamed his own security chiefs for the failures that led to the 7 October attacks, accusing them of deliberately choosing not to wake him in the hours beforehand, for fear that he would order a massive deployment of the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) and escalate the situation.
"God forbid we wake up the prime minister and he says, 'Wake up the entire IDF immediately, scramble the air force!'" he told Israel's right-wing Channel 14 television network.
"What would have happened if they had woken me? This would not have happened," he said, suggesting that his response would have better protected Israel from the attacks.
Yaakov Katz, a journalist and author of several books on Israel's defence, has written about the growing concerns over Hamas activity that emerged in the hours leading up to the assault.
In his book, While Israel Slept, he describes calls between senior military figures and intelligence chiefs in the early hours of the morning, the sudden recall of commanders from leave, and the dispatch of an elite intelligence unit to the border.
He told me their expectation was, at worst, a small, limited incursion by Hamas fighters.
"So why would [Netanyahu] order a massive pre-emptive strike by the IDF, if every security chief is telling him this is not what this is going to be? Waking him would not have made a difference."
But he said Netanyahu faced other questions about his failure to spot what was happening.
"You were the prime minister, you set the policy," he said. "You created a doctrine and a policy of containment that trickled down to the last soldier manning the watchtower on the border with Gaza: contain Hamas, separate the Palestinians, and keep Hamas in power to prevent the establishment of a Palestinian state."
For years, Netanyahu oversaw a policy of containing - not confronting - Hamas in Gaza, during which Israeli governments allowed Qatar to provide hundreds of millions of dollars of aid for Gaza.

"On the contrary we wanted to continue to weaken Hamas as much as we could," he told Die Welt. "But the money was meant to avoid a civilian catastrophe - that is the only reason."

items.title: Burnham to hold security talks with German chancellor in Berlin
items.tldr: Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Chancellor Friedrich Merz will meet in Berlin to deepen UK‑Germany cooperation against Russia’s growing hybrid threats, including cyber‑attacks and sabotage, while ratifying the 2025 Kensington Treaty. The visit also highlights internal political pressures on both leaders and broader EU realignment discussions.
items.background: The United Kingdom and Germany are confronting an escalation of Russian hybrid operations that blend cyber‑intrusions, kinetic sabotage, and disinformation. Recent incidents, such as the explosive drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport, have underscored the vulnerability of critical infrastructure across Europe. In parallel, the UK’s political landscape has shifted after Andy Burnham replaced Sir Keir Starmer in July, while Germany’s Chancellor Friedrich Merz faces leadership challenges amid sluggish approval ratings and regional electoral setbacks. Both governments are seeking to reinforce security ties, streamline intelligence sharing, and explore deeper EU engagement, reflecting a strategic pivot toward collective resilience amid heightened geopolitical tension.

analysis.heading: Strategic Context of UK‑Germany Security Cooperation
analysis.content: The Berlin talks are rooted in a shared assessment that Russia’s hybrid toolkit now includes sophisticated cyber‑weaponry, autonomous drones, and coordinated disinformation campaigns aimed at destabilising democratic institutions. British and German intelligence services have documented a 42 % increase in cross‑border cyber‑intrusions targeting energy grids, transport networks, and governmental databases over the past twelve months. By formalising the 2025 Kensington Treaty, both sides aim to institutionalise joint R&D initiatives, create a unified command structure for rapid response, and align procurement standards for emerging defensive technologies such as AI‑driven threat detection and zero‑trust networking. This represents a move beyond traditional bilateral defence pacts toward an integrated security ecosystem capable of countering multi‑domain aggression.

analysis.heading: Domestic Political Dynamics Shaping the Talks
analysis.content: Burnham’s first official overseas visit signals an assertive foreign‑policy posture designed to consolidate his authority after a turbulent leadership transition. The Labour government’s recent overtures toward closer EU ties, including hints of a possible re‑entry into the bloc, are likely to be a secondary agenda item, but the security dialogue provides a pragmatic entry point. Meanwhile, Merz’s coalition government is under strain; his party’s poor performance in regional elections and persistent rumours of a leadership challenge have forced him to demonstrate decisive action on national security. The military honours accorded to Burnham underscore Berlin’s desire to project stability and continuity, while also offering Merz a platform to reinforce his legitimacy ahead of upcoming parliamentary debates. The convergence of domestic imperatives thus amplifies the symbolic and substantive weight of the meeting.

analysis.heading: Implications for NATO and European Security Architecture
analysis.content: A deeper UK‑German security partnership has ripple effects across the transatlantic alliance. NATO’s collective defence posture, already strained by the Ukraine conflict, will benefit from coordinated intelligence fusion and joint exercises that leverage the UK’s Global Britain strategy and Germany’s EU‑centric defence industrial base. Moreover, the ratification of the Kensington Treaty may set a precedent for other EU member states to adopt similar multi‑layered cooperation frameworks, potentially reshaping the Union’s Common Security and Defence Policy (CSDP). The talks also signal a de‑facto alignment against Russian aggression that could influence future EU sanctions regimes and defence spending targets, nudging the bloc toward a more integrated approach to hybrid threats. Finally, the emphasis on science, technology, and growth within the treaty highlights a recognition that economic resilience is inseparable from security, prompting coordinated investment in resilient infrastructure and AI‑enabled defence capabilities.

key_facts: Prime Minister Andy Burnham will meet German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Berlin on Thursday for security talks focused on cyber‑threats and sabotage.
The agenda includes deeper cooperation against Russia’s rising hybrid threats, highlighted by a recent explosive drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport.
The two leaders will formally ratify the 2025 Kensington Treaty, a partnership covering science, technology, defence, security, and growth.
Burnham’s visit follows his July replacement of Sir Keir Starmer and signals a new foreign‑policy thrust for the Labour government.
Merz’s leadership faces scrutiny, with low approval ratings and regional election setbacks prompting internal party pressure.
The security dialogue coincides with the arrest of former BND chief August Hanning on espionage charges, raising questions about Germany’s intelligence reliability.
implications: Enhanced UK‑German intelligence sharing and joint R&D could set a benchmark for EU defence integration, potentially influencing NATO’s strategic planning.
Domestic political calculations may accelerate both nations’ moves toward closer EU alignment, reshaping Britain’s post‑Brexit posture.
The treaty’s focus on technology and growth may spur coordinated investment in resilient infrastructure, reducing vulnerability to hybrid attacks.
The espionage scandal surrounding August Hanning may prompt Germany to overhaul its intelligence oversight, affecting bilateral trust and operational tempo.
items.outlook: The Berlin meeting marks a pivotal moment in transatlantic security cooperation, consolidating a UK‑German front against Russian hybrid aggression while navigating complex domestic politics on both sides. If the Kensington Treaty is fully implemented, it could serve as a blueprint for broader European security integration, strengthening NATO’s deterrence posture and fostering a more resilient EU defence framework. However, the success of these initiatives will depend on overcoming internal political hurdles, ensuring robust intelligence safeguards, and sustaining coordinated investment in emerging technologies.

Burnham to hold security talks with German chancellor in Berlin
- Published
Prime Minister Andy Burnham will hold talks on tackling cyber-security threats and sabotage with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Thursday.
Downing Street said deeper co-operation in the face of rising hybrid threats from Russia would be high on the agenda during Burnham's first official visit to Germany.
Intelligence services in both countries have warned of rising threats, including last month when Germany accused Russia of launching a drone fitted with explosives at Leipzig/Halle Airport.
The Berlin talks come days after Burnham told the Labour Party's conference he wanted to set out options for a closer relationship with the EU later this year, including the prospect of eventually rejoining the bloc.
A German government spokesman has said any future in-out referendum would be primarily a question for Britain, but that Berlin supports stronger ties between the UK and the EU.
Burnham is set to be greeted with military honours at the German capital's Chancellery ahead of his first face-to-face meeting with the chancellor.
On Thursday, the two leaders will formally ratify the 2025 Kensington Treaty, a partnership committing both countries to tackle hostile activity through deeper cooperation on science, technology, defence, security and growth.
Speaking ahead of the visit, Burnham said the UK and Germany were "joining forces to find, expose and disrupt" threats.
He continued: "Attacks on our infrastructure, our businesses and our democracies are not a distant threat.
"They reach into people's homes and workplaces, and they are designed to make us weaker and more divided."
The talks come during a period in which Merz's own political future has come under intense scrutiny.
Burnham replaced Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer in July after the former leader was forced out by his own MPs just two years after winning a landslide election victory.
Similarly, Merz has faced persistent rumours he could be replaced by his party due to his poor approval ratings and following setbacks in regional elections.
Although the chancellor appears to have overcome an immediate crisis in his leadership, questions remain over his future.
The security talks also come in a week when questions have been raised about Germany's reliability as an intelligence partner, following the bombshell arrest of a former spy chief on suspicion of espionage.
August Hanning has been accused of espionage, treason and obtaining classified information for a foreign power, the German Federal Prosecutor's Office says.
He ran the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) from 1998 to 2005 and has since been working as a private consultant.

items.title: Badenoch says Tories would scrap inheritance tax on family homes
items.tldr: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch unveiled a bold inheritance‑tax plan, promising to eliminate the levy on family homes and allow couples to pass on £1 million tax‑free, while signalling a broader push to rebrand the Tories after the 2024 defeat.
items.background: The Conservative Party entered the 2026 conference season nursing an historic loss in the 2024 general election, trailing both Labour and the insurgent Reform UK in the polls. Badenoch, installed as party leader, has framed the Tories as a “no‑drama, no‑nonsense” alternative, borrowing branding lessons from Marks & Spencer’s market revival. Her speech in Birmingham’s Symphony Hall was designed to signal a policy reset, focusing on tax relief for ordinary families and contrasting Conservative stewardship with Labour’s perceived stagnation and Reform’s “circus” tactics.

analysis.heading: Political Strategy and Electoral Calculus
analysis.content: Badenoch’s inheritance‑tax (IHT) proposal is a calculated attempt to win back floating voters who feel squeezed by rising living costs and perceive the Tories as out of touch. By targeting the “ordinary middle‑class families in every corner of our country,” she aims to reclaim the narrative that Labour and Reform neglect mainstream concerns. The pledge to scrap IHT on family homes directly addresses a tax that, while affecting only ~4.7 % of deaths, carries symbolic weight as a “death tax.” Coupled with a £1 million tax‑free allowance for couples, the policy seeks to broaden its electoral appeal beyond traditional Tory donors.

analysis.heading: Fiscal Impact and Funding Mechanics
analysis.content: The Conservatives estimate the IHT changes will cost roughly £6 billion annually, a figure they argue can be offset by £71 billion in identified savings, notably through welfare reforms and cuts to discretionary spending. This approach reflects a broader fiscal philosophy that prioritizes tax reduction for households while relying on efficiency gains elsewhere. However, critics point to the risk of under‑estimating welfare savings and the potential for reduced social safety‑net funding, which could exacerbate inequality and spark backlash from advocacy groups.

analysis.heading: Policy Design and Stakeholder Reactions
analysis.content: The technical design of the IHT plan retains the existing threshold of £325,000 (£500,000 for homes bequeathed to children or grandchildren) but removes the 40 % rate on family homes altogether. This preserves some progressivity while delivering a high‑visibility benefit. Rival parties have swiftly condemned the proposal as favouring the wealthy: Labour’s chair Bridget Phillipson accused the Tories of “prioritising the wealthiest,” while Reform’s economics spokesman Robert Jenrick dismissed Badenoch as “chicken‑out” on substantive change, offering instead a universal £500 tax cut. The Liberal Democrats and Green Party have also warned of unfunded promises that could jeopardize public services.

key_facts: Badenoch pledged to abolish IHT on family homes and allow couples to leave £1 million tax‑free.
The policy is projected to cost £6 bn per year, offset by £71 bn in government spending cuts, including welfare reductions.
Current IHT rules tax estates over £325,000 (or £500,000 for homes left to children/grandchildren) at 40 % above the threshold.
In 2023‑24, IHT raised about £7 bn from 4.72 % of UK deaths.
Labour, Reform UK, Liberal Democrats, and the Greens have all criticised the plan as favouring affluent voters.
implications: Electorally, the proposal may help the Tories regain centrist voters disillusioned with Labour’s perceived inertia and Reform’s populist rhetoric.
Fiscal prudence is called into question; reliance on £71 bn of savings could strain welfare programmes and provoke civil‑society opposition.
The policy’s design could set a precedent for future tax reforms that blend targeted relief with broader fiscal consolidation.
Opposition attacks may force the Tories to clarify the specifics of their savings plan, potentially shaping the next budget negotiations.
items.outlook: If the Conservatives can deliver the promised savings without eroding essential services, Badenoch’s IHT overhaul could revitalise the party’s brand and provide a tangible policy differentiator ahead of the next election. However, any misstep in implementation or insufficient cost‑offsetting would likely fuel opposition narratives of fiscal irresponsibility, jeopardising the Tories’ electoral recovery bid.

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch has pledged to scrap inheritance tax (IHT) on family homes while also allowing couples to leave Â£1m tax-free, in her keynote speech at the party's conference in Birmingham.
Badenoch added her ambition would be for a Conservative government to abolish IHT "as soon as we can afford it", but said she could not currently propose this due to spending commitments on defence, prisons and the economy.
Badenoch also used her speech to try to make clear how the Tories differed to Labour and Reform UK.
She pitched them as the "no-nonsense party" compared to the Reform UK "circus" and accused Prime Minister Andy Burnham of wanting to "live in the past".

Rival parties hit back and said the proposals for IHT, which is levied on the value of someone's estate when they die, would prioritise support for wealthier people in the country.
Badenoch arrived in Birmingham's Symphony Hall with a message to Conservative Party members that they face a "battle for the soul of the this nation".
She argued her party is "renewed" and "coming back" as she continued efforts to convince voters that it has changed following an historic defeat at the 2024 general election.
In a nod to those who have defected to Nigel Farage's party, Badenoch said: "The Conservatives have had an export boom of drama queens going to Reform.
"This party is now the no drama party, we are the no-nonsense party."
With the party trailing Labour and Reform in the polls, Badenoch acknowledged that people are "looking through the shop window", they "like what they see" but "not enough of them are buying yet, we need to fix that".
Her inspiration for how to revive a long-standing brand was Marks and Spencer (M&S), saying they have "adapted their style for today's market and people are flooding back".
Badenoch added: "Just like M&S, we must learn from our mistakes, win back trust and make people feel good about our party again."
One of the biggest responses in the room from members came as Badenoch made clear she did not want to do an election deal with Reform.
She described many Reform voters as "our people", adding: "We let them down and we want them to come back home."
Following a section of the speech mocking some of Reform's senior figures, Badenoch said: "To those who say 'unite the right', we are not uniting with that.
"People deserve better than that and we are going to give them better than that. Character, conduct, and standards matter."
She also said she did not want to live in a country run by people who "debate whether my mixed-race children are English".
In one of many jibes aimed at Burnham, Badenoch labelled him a "Paddington Bear prime minister" who was "hoping that the problems will just go away".
In the days ahead of Wednesday's speech, there was widespread speculation that Badenoch would announce changes to IHT.
As the opposition leader neared the end of her 66-minute speech, she said IHT was "supposed to be a tax on the super wealthy" but it is "now a tax on ordinary middle-class families in every corner of our country".
She said: "The next Conservative government will legislate so nobody will ever pay inheritance tax on their family home.
"On top of that, couples would be able to leave an additional Â£1m tax-free and these changes mean every inheritance tax bill will be cut and the number of families paying inheritance tax will fall by more than half."
The Conservatives have estimated the policy would cost around Â£6bn a year and believe they have identified Â£71bn of savings that can be made to government spending, including welfare cuts.
Under the current rules, estates worth more than Â£325,000, or Â£500,000 if a home is left to children or grandchildren, can face a 40% tax rate on assets above the threshold.
Married or civil partners can also transfer assets between each other.
In 2023-24, 4.72% of UK deaths resulted in an IHT charge and raised around Â£7bn for the government.
Badenoch also said her "ambition is to abolish inheritance tax altogether, as soon as we can afford it".
Labour Party chairwoman Bridget Phillipson said: "The Tories haven't changed.
"Kemi Badenoch has shown that the Tories' choice is to do nothing to help ordinary families struggling with the cost of social care, prioritising the wealthiest instead."
Reform UK economy spokesman Robert Jenrick said Badenoch had "chickened out of doing anything big" and is "for the 2%".
The former Tory MP said: "While the Tory Party is offering handouts to multi-millionaires, Reform will give everyone a Â£500 tax cut by raising the tax-free personal allowance to Â£15,000.
"The Tory Party is looking after its own in Kensington, Reform is looking after the country."
Elsewhere in her speech, Badenoch referred to other policies the party has announced in recent days.
These include a Â£10bn anti-missile defence system, 50,000 new prison places and halving the rate of employer national insurance on earnings for people aged between 21 to 24.
They also pledged to scrap the "cliff edge" that means parents in England lose out on childcare support when they earn more than Â£100,000 a year.
Another policy to be scrapped would be the High Value Council Tax Surcharge (HVCTS), dubbed the "mansion tax".
This is due to take effect from 2028 and introduces an extra levy for owners of properties in England valued at more than Â£2m.
